accuracy.note: On fictional test data, 19 Nov 2026, for the 7 agents behind the four engagements (bank reconciliation, three-way match, expenses, access review, refunds and chargebacks, migration tie-out, duplicate vendors) of 30. The clean sets were written by the same author as the rules. The 1099 readiness agent is not measured: a clean vendor needs a well-formed taxpayer id, and the test files use invalid placeholders on purpose. The other 23 agents are checked by their eval cases only (596 expected markers, all found). This pass also fixed two bank-file reading bugs found on public files, two file-reading bugs found by the eight-language check, and one place where full tax ids reached the AI model.

human_review: Each system owner decides keep or revoke for every flagged account; revoking access is a one-click request a named person approves, and the agents never change access themselves.
A person reviews the reason code, the evidence list and the response draft before anything is submitted; a refund is always a person's click.
The controller and the implementation lead decide whether untied totals, missing records and duplicate masters block go-live; go-live approval is never given by an agent.

The accountant reviews matches, reconciling items, match exceptions, expense recommendations and the 1099 list, and posts any adjusting entry in the books; nothing is posted, paid or filed by the agents.
common_problems: Bank fees and interest not booked, and checks and deposits not yet cleared, listed as reconciling items with a draft adjusting entry.
Invoices billed above the receipt or the PO price, duplicate invoices, invoices with no PO or no receipt.
Expense lines over the policy limit, with no receipt, sent late, without pre-approval, or claimed twice.
Vendors paid over the 1099 threshold with no W-9, an unsigned or old W-9, or a malformed taxpayer id.
People who left the company but still have access, admin accounts without MFA, shared accounts and service accounts with no owner.
Refund requests outside the return window, over the refundable amount, duplicated, or for an order that does not exist.
Migration loads where records are missing, amounts changed or totals do not tie with the old system.
Duplicate vendor records that share a tax id, phone or address.
reaches_the_model: When an assistant calls a tool, its model sees the result: amounts, dates, ids, finding codes and text from your files, including people's names and e-mail addresses (Fairbooks has no general masking, unlike the newer Fair families). Masked: taxpayer ids (last four digits), secrets found in configuration and automation exports, card numbers in receipt text, and the person in an erasure request. The report and draft files written on your computer hold the full values. Results go to whatever model your assistant uses; for staff, customer and vendor data, use a model covered by your own agreements or a local model.
rules_maintained: Rules that change are settings or dated files, and a result names what it used: the 1099 threshold by tax year (600 before 2026, 2,000 in 2026, later years marked for confirmation), taxpayer id patterns, the cookie and tracker vendor list (version 2026.11.0), the MCP package advisory snapshot (2026-11-15), license text fingerprints and certificate strength rules. Expense, refund, tolerance, retention and access policies are your own JSON files, checked against a schema. You edit those files yourself, or support updates the bundled lists when a rule or a vendor changes.
